payload.title: Travel Advisor Benefits You Cannot Get Booking Alone
payload.audience: 30s, couples who are interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, 150k+ AUD budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a budget of AUD 150k or more, planning a destination wedding and honeymoon, who are used to booking their own travel and are weighing whether a travel advisor is worth it, and want a plain, honest account of what an advisor actually takes off their plate, what they can still do themselves, and what to ask any advisor before they agree to work together.
payload.goal: Speak with a Wedded Advisor: request a Wedded Concierge consultation at /wonderland-concierge so one advisor can plan the venue, travel, vendors and payments for the wedding abroad.
payload.angle: Page-one results for 'travel advisor benefits' are mostly agency and host-agency sales pages that promise upgrades, perks, insider rates and exclusive access, often US-centric and unsourced. This guide makes no perk claims at all. It frames 'cannot get booking alone' honestly as the things that are harder or slower to arrange yourself once a trip becomes a destination wedding: one point of contact across flights, stays and the wedding; quotes in AUD; inclusions confirmed in writing before you commit; someone working in your time zone; venue, travel, vendors and payments planned together. Each Wedded Advisor point is stated only in brand-facts.md wording, and any general benefit (accreditation, consumer protections, what to check before paying) is stated only as ACCC, the ATAS accreditation scheme, Smartraveller and Moneysmart state it. It then gives the reader what sales pages never do: an honest split of what you can do yourself versus where it gets harder (guests, many suppliers, payments in several currencies, posed as questions to ask yourself, not claims), and a checklist of questions to ask any advisor (accreditation, fee in writing, inclusions, cancellation terms, insurance).
must_include: Intro with a direct answer in the first 100 words: a good travel advisor's main benefit for a destination wedding is one person coordinating flights, stays and the wedding, with costs and inclusions confirmed in writing; framed as easier and faster, never exclusive or superior. Then exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways (one point of contact across the whole trip and the wedding; quotes in AUD and inclusions confirmed in writing before you commit; you can still book plenty yourself, and the harder parts are guests, many suppliers and several currencies; ask any advisor about accreditation, the fee in writing, inclusions, cancellation terms and insurance before you agree).

What a travel advisor does: general description of coordination and booking on your behalf; any general statement about the role, accreditation or consumer rights only as ACCC, ATAS, Smartraveller or Moneysmart state it [[VERIFY: wording and source]].

The benefits, each as its own short subsection, Wedded Advisor points in brand-facts.md wording only: (1) one point of contact across flights, stays and the wedding ('One Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact.'); (2) quotes in AUD ('Advisor works in the couple's time zone and quotes in AUD for Australian couples.'); (3) inclusions in writing ('The advisor confirms inclusions in writing before the couple commits.' Inclusions only, never house rules or availability); (4) your time zone (same brand-facts line); (5) venue, travel, vendors and payments planned together ('Plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world.'); (6) accreditation and consumer protections only as the official sources state them [[VERIFY: ATAS accreditation scope; ACCC consumer guarantees for travel services; Moneysmart and Smartraveller guidance]]. Fee agreed in writing before work begins may appear in the questions section ('The fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.').

What you can do yourself and where it gets harder: affirm that many couples book flights and stays themselves; then pose questions, not claims (Who tracks guest travel and room needs? Who keeps many suppliers' dates and terms aligned? How will you handle payments in several currencies and who tracks them?). No statistics, no scare framing.

Questions to ask any advisor, as a numbered checklist: Are you accredited, and with which scheme (ATAS as the scheme states) [[VERIFY]]? Is the fee agreed in writing before work begins? Which inclusions will you confirm in writing? What are the cancellation and change terms for each booking? What travel insurance should we consider (pointing to Smartraveller guidance) [[VERIFY]]? Neutral: applies to any advisor.

Destination weddings and honeymoons: how the same benefits apply when the trip is a wedding plus a honeymoon; carries the ONLY Advisor line in the body (brand-facts wording, e.g. 'One Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact.') with the /wonderland-concierge link (anchor 'Wedded Concierge'); links /destination-wedding-packages, /destination-packages and one Greece cluster guide (/destination-weddings/greece-wedding-packages, fallback /destinations/europe/greece) as examples of where couples plan, without venue or price detail; /travel as the travel hub.

FAQ (4 to 6): What does a travel advisor do? Is a travel advisor worth it for a destination wedding? Can I book some things myself and use an advisor for the rest? What is ATAS accreditation? Do travel advisors quote in Australian dollars? What should I ask before hiring a travel advisor? Answers from the same sources as the body; ATAS and consumer answers only as the official source states.

Close: the one Advisor line from brand-facts.md (never the Wedded Advisor definition line or 'last dance'). Links /wonderland-concierge (Wedded Concierge) and /magazine as the magnet. UTMs utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=travel-advisor-benefits&utm_content=primary|secondary|magnet|closing on /wonderland-concierge and /magazine only.
avoid: Perks of any kind: upgrades, credits, preferred or insider rates, VIP amenities, 'better deals', 'exclusive access', 'free', room-block benefits.
Wedded Privileges (deferred; /privileges is a 404) and the brand-facts line about guest room blocks with Wedded Privileges.
Transfers, availability promises, house rules, or 'actually free' dates language from the Concierge steps.
Legal, church, religious or marriage paperwork help implied for the advisor.
Business details that are deferred: commission or fee basis, who is on the ground, number of weddings or years, scale proof, named advisor, phone line, call-first.
'Cannot get booking alone' framed as exclusivity or superiority over the reader; it means harder or slower to arrange yourself.
General advisor benefits from any source other than ACCC, ATAS, Smartraveller or Moneysmart, and anything beyond what those sources state.
Any price, fee amount, saving, percentage or amount.
Vendor, hotel, airline, consortium, agency, host agency or competitor names; competitor wording or images; Easy Weddings.
'Best' or ranking language; more than one Advisor line in the body besides the close; the Advisor definition line; 'last dance'; 'Wonderland Concierge' as anchor text.
Research talk ('we could not confirm', 'according to our research'); per-line source credits; hedge stacking; statistics.
Clichés, exclamation marks, keywords pasted into headings, em dashes, US spelling.
